title: The night sky
hook: the stars you can see are only the nearest few

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fajr and the sunrise. Your line was it arrives. Today, the other end of the day.

Step out of a lit kitchen into a dark yard and, at first, there's almost nothing up there. A few bright points. Maybe a plane. Give it a few minutes. Your eyes adjust, and more stars come out, faint ones between the bright ones, until the sky that looked empty looks crowded. Yet every one of those stars, even on the darkest night, is close by, as stars go. Neighbors. The ones you can see with your own eyes are only the nearest few.
screen: `OUT OF A LIT KITCHEN.` → `GIVE IT A FEW MINUTES.` → `ONLY THE NEAREST FEW.`

segments.voice: First, the size of what you're seeing. Astronomers say the stars visible to the naked eye all belong to our own galaxy, and to a small nearby part of it. Beyond them lie stars too faint to see, and beyond those, other galaxies. The night sky you can see is the front porch of something far larger. Second, the light. Starlight takes time to cross space, so each point is light that left its star long before tonight. You're looking at the past, from many different moments at once. Third, two old texts that looked up and heard different things. In the book of Job, the voice from the whirlwind turns the stars into questions Job can't answer. In the King James words: "Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?" The stars become a lesson in what Job cannot do. A psalm looks up at the same sky and asks its own question: "When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" And the psalm answers that this small creature is crowned with glory and honor. Humbled, and held. Both reactions are honest, and both start with someone standing still long enough to feel their size. Fourth, why it's a practice and not just a fact. You can read that the visible stars are only the nearest. It lands differently in a dark yard, neck tipped back, as the sky keeps filling in the longer you stay.
screen: `THE NEAREST PART OF OUR GALAXY.` · `LIGHT THAT LEFT LONG AGO.` · `JOB'S STARS, THE PSALM'S QUESTION.` · `THE SKY FILLS IN AS YOU STAY.` · then, large: `WHAT IS MAN, THAT THOU ART MINDFUL OF HIM?`

segments.voice: If it's dark, go to a window or door, turn off the lights behind you and look up; if it's daytime, close your eyes and bring back the darkest night sky you've seen. Don't look for anything in particular; let the sky fill in, one more faint star with each breath. If you pray, you can let the psalm's question be part of your prayer.
Pleiades. One of the star clusters named in the book of Job, a reminder that every star you can see is a near neighbor, light from the past. Today's word.
Your line: the nearest stars. Humbled, and held, under one and the same sky. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: People who practice stargazing as a practice of awe find a dark place away from lights, let their eyes adjust for several minutes, and look up without hurrying; some read Psalm 8, Job 38 or another text under the sky.

notes: Editor: cut the stock 'here's the strange part'; dropped 'notice your own size' from the practice (the small self ran on days 1030 and 1032); softened 'puts Job in his place'; myth item no longer says Psalm 8 ends at the crowning (it ends with praise); corrected the Pascal day reference in notes.

Astronomy claims are kept qualitative (no distances or star counts): naked-eye stars belong to a nearby part of our galaxy; starlight left its star before tonight. The Andromeda galaxy can be seen as a faint smudge by the naked eye; the script speaks of stars, not galaxies, so the myth item says stars in other galaxies — confirm that wording is accurate enough.
Psalm 8:5 ('crowned him with glory and honour') is paraphrased with American spelling; confirm.
Job 38:31 quoted from memory; confirm wording. Pascal's 'eternal silence' line was deliberately not used (already on day 1016).
Avoids the Kant (day 1017) and Sagan (day 1026) angles on the stars.
